title: Radical amazement
hook: Abraham Joshua Heschel called for radical amazement at the ordinary (God in Search of Man)

segments.voice: Yesterday, William James, and moments hard to put into words. Your line was hard to say. This week went from mountains and Darwin to star stuff and the numinous: big things, mostly. Today a rabbi turns toward the small.

A faucet. Turn the handle and clean water comes out, cold or hot, whenever you like. A light switch. A slice of bread. The fact that you woke up this morning, your heart having kept going all night without being asked. None of this makes the news, or gets a second look. Abraham Joshua Heschel, a Jewish teacher and rabbi, thought that missing second look was one of the deepest problems a person can have. And he had a name for the cure.
screen: `THE FAUCET. THE SWITCH. THE BREAD.` → `NO SECOND LOOK.` → `HESCHEL NAMES THE CURE.`

segments.voice: The name is radical amazement, from his book God in Search of Man. First, what he meant. Not amazement at the unusual, comets, miracles, record-breaking anything, but at the usual: at the plain fact that there is anything at all, instead of nothing. Radical, in the sense of going all the way to the root. Second, what it's up against. People grow used to the world, Heschel wrote, and taking it for granted is no small mistake. He called indifference to the sublime wonder of living the root of sin. Strong words from a gentle writer. For him, losing wonder wasn't a mood problem; it was a way of going blind. Third, where he found the practice. Heschel stood inside Jewish tradition, which has blessings for ordinary moments: on waking, on eating bread, on seeing lightning, on hearing thunder. He saw blessing as a way of refusing to take things for granted, out loud, many times a day. A much older line in the Psalms has the same posture. In the King James words: "I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works." Fourth, what it asks of anyone, religious or not: not a trip somewhere spectacular, but a second look at what's already in your hand. Heschel believed wonder was where awareness of God begins. Others who don't share his faith borrow the phrase anyway, because the ordinary is still sitting there, waiting to be noticed.
screen: `AMAZED AT THE USUAL.` · `INDIFFERENCE IS A KIND OF BLINDNESS.` · `BLESSINGS FOR ORDINARY MOMENTS.` · `A SECOND LOOK AT WHAT'S IN YOUR HAND.` · then, large: `FEARFULLY AND WONDERFULLY MADE.`

segments.voice: Pick up one ordinary thing within reach, a cup, a key, a spoon, and look at it as if it had just been handed to you for the first time: who made it, and what had to happen for it to be here? Then take Heschel's step and notice that it exists at all. If you pray, you can let this looking become a blessing in your own tradition's words.
Radical amazement. Abraham Joshua Heschel's phrase for wonder at the ordinary, all the way to the root: that anything is here at all. Today's word.
Your line: fearfully and wonderfully made. Amazed at the usual, all the way to the root. A week of wonder, complete.

howItsDone: Readers of Heschel often connect radical amazement to Jewish blessings said over ordinary moments, such as waking, eating bread, or seeing lightning; others take the phrase as an invitation to look again at everyday things.
